3. 
Borders, Immigrants, and Due Process. Procedural and substantive 
due process analysis has proved awkward in the immigration context, where 
the demise of the “right/privilege” distinction made it harder for courts to 
deploy a simple framework that would ostensibly answer questions about the 
scope of due process rights of non-citizens. Where the right to immigrate was 
once categorically treated as a “privilege” and aliens were therefore viewed as 
having limited if any constitutional rights in any instance, courts have now 
come to treat aliens differently depending on their situation and location. 
Ahens seeking admission at the border are understood to lack a due process 
interest in challenging a decision to find them inadmissible. Meanwhile, court 
decisions recognize that even unlawfully present aliens (within the borders of 
the United States) as well as returning legal residents are entitled to 
procedural due process regarding expulsion or denial of entry. See, e.g.. Bridges 
V. Wixon, 326 U.S. 135 (1945); Landon v. Plasencia, 459 U.S. 21 (1982). 
Penalties deemed to be punishment or not sufficiently related to enforcing 
removal may violate substantive due process. See, e.g., Wong Wing v. United 
States, 163 U.S. 228 (1896); Zadvydas v. Davis, 533 U.S. 687 (2001). The 
question of what procedures are appropriate as a matter of statutory and 
constitutional law for aliens facing removal is generally governed by the 
Mathews v. Eldridge test. See, e.g.. United States v. Raya-Vaca, 771 F.3d 1195 
(9th Cir. 2014) (due process requires advising a noncitizen of charges against 
him).
4. 
Due Process, Statutory Construction, and the Rights of Aliens. Due 
process concerns may color judicial construction of statutory hearing rights, as 
Section A of this chapter illustrated. Due process analysis also affects statutory 
construction through the “constitutional avoidance” canon—and disputes over 
the extent of procedural due process protections for aliens have provided some 
prominent examples. Courts have had to resolve disputes, for example, about 
the impact of statutes on the possibility of recourse to habeas corpus or other 
forms of judicial review for aliens ordered removed. During the mid-1990s. 
Congress enacted a number of statutes, including the Antiterrorism and 
Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA) and the Illegal Immigration Reform and 
Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA), seeking to limit aliens’ access to 
Article III courts. The Supreme Court has nonetheless read the relevant 
provisions of AEDPA and IIRIRA in a manner that avoids the need to resolve 
the question of the limits of congressional power to restrict federal courts’ 
ability to review the deportation of non-citizens. See INS v. St. Cyr, 533 U.S. 
289 (2001) (finding that some judicial review of deportation orders is required 
by the Suspension Clause and preserving of access to an Article III court to 
review legal and constitutional claims avoids serious constitutional questions); 
Calcano-Martinez v. INS, 533 U.S. 348 (2001) (same); Zadvydas v. Davis, 533 
U.S. 687 (2001) (recognizing availabiLity of habeas corpus and imposing limits 
on post-removal detention to avoid constitutional concerns). These cases 
highlight the extent to which decisions involving the constitutional rights of 
non-citizens, particularly those subject to removal proceedings, can turn on 
constitutional concerns that drive statutory construction.
